extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military commanders, military legal officers, and scholars interpreting the Articles of War
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive guidance and legal standards for applying specific Articles of War (desertion, reenlistment, advising/persuading to desert, attendance at divine service, stoppage of pay for damages, surrender to civil authorities, embezzlement and related offenses). Aimed at commanders and military lawyers deciding applicability, procedure, and limits of the Articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII B — Waiver of liability for deserter's lost time
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States may waive the liability imposed by the first clause of the article. It is waived where the deserter, without being required to perform the service, is discharged by one of the officials authorized by article 4 to discharge soldiers; and where the soldier is adjudged to be dishonorably discharged by sentence of court-martial, duly approved and executed. A deserter who has been duly discharged from the service does not remain amenable to trial under the last clause of this article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations of opinions and practice (R. 29, 607; 30, 506; 37, 416; R. 31, 48) are given as supporting examples of waiver and related administrative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII C1 — Operative requirement to make good time after court-martial without discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a conviction by court-martial for desertion where the sentence does not include discharge, the requirement to make good time lost becomes operative by its own force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C. 16814 (Nov. 13 and Dec. 4, 1906). This treats reenlistment of unpaid time as an independent obligation triggered even if discharge was not adjured in the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII C2 — Liability to make good time independent of court-martial punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The liability to make good to the United States the time lost by desertion, enjoined by the first clause of this article, is independent of any punishment which may be imposed by a court-martial on conviction of the offense; it need not, therefore, be adjudged or mentioned in terms in a sentence. If the sentence is disapproved, the legal status of the accused is the same as if he had been acquitted, and the obligation of additional service is not incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: R. 50, 413 (June, 1886); R. 26, 668 (June, 1868) — examples and explanatory holdings clarify independence of civil obligation from punitive adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII C3 — Enforcement postponed until execution of punishment; applicability after enlistment expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement of the liability is postponed until after the execution of the punishment (if any) imposed by sentence. A deserter may still be required to make good the time included in his unauthorized absence from the service, although his term of enlistment has expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: R. 32, 40 (Oct., 1871); C. 18492 (Aug. 31, 1905) illustrate postponement and enforcement even post-enlistment.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII C4 — Disapproval of conviction operates as acquittal as to making good time
rubrics_metrics.description: As the disapproval of a conviction operates as an acquittal, a soldier whose conviction of desertion has been disapproved by the reviewing authority cannot be required to make good time lost in desertion under the forty-eighth article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited controlling opinions: C. 16814 (Apr. 11, 1907); 18438 (June 26, 1908); 18438 (Aug. 3, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII D — Character of liability to make good time is penal; wiped out on acquittal
rubrics_metrics.description: The provision that a deserter must make good time lost in desertion is penal in character. If the soldier is acquitted of desertion, the liability to make good the time lost is wiped out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C. 16814 (Dec. 4, 1906). Emphasizes penal nature and consequence of acquittal.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII E — Liability requires actual military service and excludes time awaiting trial or serving sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that a deserter shall be liable to serve such period as will with the time he may have served previous to his desertion amount to full time of his enlistment requires military service and excludes from the computation time spent while awaiting trial or serving sentence. The deserter does not begin to serve the unexecuted portion until he has completed his sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple authorities cited (R. 30, 606; 31, 275; 374; 16306; 16423; 17937; 21037; 21636) provide examples and reinforce the rule that only active service counts toward making up enlistment time.

rubrics_metrics.name: XLVIII F — Limitation of prosecutions and survival of make-good-time liability despite statute of limitations to desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability to trial and punishment imposed by the second clause of the article is subject to the limitation of prosecutions prescribed in the one hundred and third article of war. Held further that the liability to make good time lost in desertion continues even though the statute of limitation has taken effect or been successfully pleaded in bar as to the desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: R. 31, 384; C. 15257; May 3, 1910; R. 37, 416; P. 48 and 69 (Mar., 1890) — demonstrates distinction between criminal prosecution limits and administrative/service obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: I A — Reenlistment as prima facie evidence of desertion, not itself desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: This article's first clause does not create a new offense but declares that a soldier who abandons his regiment shall be deemed a deserter although he may forthwith reenlist in a new regiment. Reenlistment does not render the act of reenlistment a desertion, but simply makes reenlistment prima facie evidence of desertion from the previous enlistment from which the soldier has not been discharged, or evidence of intent not to return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical purpose traced to British Code; numerous precedents cited (R. 42, 642; P.7, 298; cases through 24722) illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: LI A — Advising vs persuading to desert: mens rea and act distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration by one soldier to another of willingness to desert with him is not 'advising to desert' in the sense of the article. To constitute the offense of advising to desert, actual desertion by the party advised is not essential; but to constitute persuading to desert, the persuasion should have induced the act (i.e., actual desertion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority R. 39, 407 (Jan., 1878); opinion C. 23215 (May 8, 1908) — clarifies distinction between mere talk, advising, and persuasion with inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: III A — No authority to force religious attendance as part of military formation
rubrics_metrics.description: A post commander has no authority under the fifty-second article of war to require soldiers to march to church and participate in divine worship as part of a military formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in C. 20968 (Jan. 19, 1907) — plain rule limiting commander authority re religious exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: III B — Attendance at divine service recommended; travel to/from service constitutes 'on duty' for medical care
rubrics_metrics.description: The fifty-second article contains a recommendation that officers and soldiers diligently attend divine service. Held that an officer or soldier so engaged, while on his way to or returning from such service, is 'on duty' within the meaning of the medical care act (Act of April 23, 1904) providing medical care and treatment to officers and enlisted men on duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 17045 (Oct. 25, 1904) is cited as example; ties attendance to entitlements under other statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV A — Strict construction of 54th article's specific redress; extends to property by American authority
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sound construction to extend the specific measure of redress contained in the fifty-fourth article of war beyond the specified cases; its strict construction limits specific redress to acts of violence against a person. However, American authority extends it further to acts of violence against property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (R.7,263; P.37,293; C. 4537; 8043; 15180; 20543; 22357) demonstrate scope and the prevailing American extension to property damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV B — Mandatory nature of 54th article and pro rata stoppage when offenders not identifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: This article is mandatory in its terms; the harsh and summary action required of the commanding officer must be applied to all cases falling within its scope. Where proper complaint presented, orders/regulations complied with, and offenders' names cannot be ascertained but substantially the entire enlisted membership participated, stoppage was made pro rata against them and held within scope of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: C. 13106 (Aug. 22, 1902) — shows application when identification impossible and command-wide participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV C — Stoppage may be assessed against entire command when active perpetrators cannot be found
rubrics_metrics.description: Where complaint was duly made and active perpetrators could not be found upon investigation, but the entire command was present and implicated, stoppages may legally be made against all individuals present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: R.8,671; 12,673; 50,9; C.1861; 6839; 13106; 24491; 26836 — examples of assessing collective liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV C1 — Exceptions to assessment for personnel whose duties precluded presence
rubrics_metrics.description: When an entire command was assessed, those men whose duties were such as to preclude the belief they were present at commission of the act (members of the guard, sick in hospital, men in confinement, absent on duty, etc.) should be excepted from assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19196 (Feb. 13, 1906) provides explicit categories of exempted personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV D1 — Reparation under article unaffected by separate criminal liability or civil punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not affect the question of reparation under the article that the offender(s) may be criminally liable for the injury or may have been punished by civil authorities for the same act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 34, 335 (June, 1873); C. 22357 (Nov. 15, 1907) cited as support.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV D2 — Distinction between stoppage and punishment by fine; interaction with forfeiture of pay
rubrics_metrics.description: The stoppage contemplated is distinct from a punishment by fine and cannot affect the question of summary reparation that the offender(s) may have already been tried and sentenced to forfeiture of pay. Forfeiture, as to its execution, properly takes precedence of stoppage; conversely, where stoppage is first properly ordered, it precedes a subsequently adjudged forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: R.21,447; C.8043; 21157 — guidance on ordering and sequencing of administrative stoppage vs judicial forfeiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV E X — Court-martial not substitute for board mandated to assess damages
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial could not properly be substituted for the board directed by General Order 35 (Headquarters of Army, 1868) to assess the amount of the damage as an agency for assessing damages under the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 37, 52 (Oct., 1875); O. 21157 (Mar. 2, 1907) — instructs procedural channel for damage assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV F1/F2 — Procedure for invoking 54th article: complaint under oath, evidence, board assessment, commander cannot act sua sponte; militia cases referred to state authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: aggrieved citizen tenders a complaint under oath charging injury against particular soldiers (named if known) with evidence. If satisfactory, the commanding officer has damages assessed by a board and orders stoppage of pay sufficient for reparation. The commander must have a proper case presented and cannot proceed sua sponte. Where requirements violated by organized militia enlisted men in joint encampment, case should be referred to regimental commander for submission to the state governor for redress under state law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive list of supporting authorities (R. 40 U; C.1861; 4768; 5347; 5586; 6839; 9766; 13106; 14971; 19196; 21157; 23148) illustrate process and the limitation on military-initiated action.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV G — Territorial applicability of 54th article (Cuba and Philippine Islands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that the fifty-fourth article of war is enforceable in Cuba and in the Philippine Islands (at date of opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 9677 (Jan. 28, 1901) is cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV H1 — 54th article not enforceable in favor of military persons or the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedial provision of the fifty-fourth article cannot be enforced in favor of military persons or in favor of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 26, 352; 27,453; 32,152; C. 8043; 23148; R. 26, 37; C. 20273; 21148 — cases showing limits on who may invoke the remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIV H2 — 54th article cannot indemnify for stolen or embezzled property
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedial provision of the fifty-fourth article cannot be invoked to indemnify persons for property stolen or embezzled.

rubrics_metrics.name: LVIII A — Military court jurisdiction concurrent (not exclusive) with civil tribunals; 'shall' construed as 'may'
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction conferred upon military courts by the article is not exclusive but concurrent with civil tribunals. The word 'shall' in 'shall be punishable' is construed as equivalent to 'may.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 4916 (Sept., 1898) and related authorities support concurrent jurisdiction interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: LVIII B — Court-martial sentences must not be less severe than local law; may be greater; court guided by local law where required
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sentence by a court convened under this article imposed punishment less severe than that provided by the law of the State where offense committed (e.g., imprisonment where state law requires death), such sentence was unauthorized and inoperative. While punishment must not be less, it may legally be of greater severity than local statute. The court, in imposing punishment, should be governed by the local law insofar as required by the article even if offense committed in state of war/insurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.2,564; R.21,77; R.21,6; C.12646 — examples and caveats when local statutory penalties differ from court-martial penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: LVIII C — Local laws of foreign country in US military occupation are not 'laws of any State' for article purposes; punishment discretionary
rubrics_metrics.description: Local laws of a foreign country in the military occupation of the United States are not 'laws of any State, Territory, or District of the United States' within the meaning of this article; at such times and places punishment for enumerated offenses would be discretionary with the court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 5267 (Nov., 1898); 5848 (Feb., 1899) illustrate treatment of occupation contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: LVIII D — Personnel in Philippine Islands during military occupation not amenable to civil courts for enumerated offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers and enlisted men of the Army serving in the Philippine Islands during the period of military occupation were held not amenable to the jurisdiction of civil courts for any of the offenses enumerated in the fifty-eighth article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.13770 (Feb. 18, 1903) provides controlling example.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX A — Subordination of military to civil power; purpose to facilitate local civil statute execution; surrender exemptions in war
rubrics_metrics.description: This article recognizes the subordination of the military to the civil power; its main purpose is to facilitate, in cases of offenders against local civil statutes connected with the Army, the execution of those statutes where such persons remain legally amenable as citizens. Protection from civil arrest is not the object. Surrenders under this article are exempted from its operation in time of war (but surrender in proper case in time of war not forbidden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple authorities (P.54,33; 63,406; C.638; 5635; 17640; 17824; 18339; 25219) used to explain policy and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX B — Requirements for civil application before surrender: specificity, identification, sworn application or warrant preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Before surrendering the party, commanding officer entitled to require that the 'application' be sufficiently specific to identify the accused and show he is charged with a particular crime within the article. Where doubt exists whether application is in good faith, commander may demand explicit sworn application and preferably a due and formal warrant or writ for arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: R.21,567; 23,490; 35,357; 53,442; C.10107; 18518; 24097; 25219 — instruct commanders on standards for accepting civil demands and protecting against bad-faith requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX C — Article applies only to crimes punishable by 'laws of the land' including municipal ordinances
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions apply only when the officer or soldier is accused of a crime or offense 'which is punishable by the laws of the land' (laws of the particular State or Territory, the United States, or common law recognized there). The by-laws or ordinances of a town or city are part of the 'laws of the land' within the meaning of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.35,357; P.63,406; cited Attorney General Olney opinion and supporting authorities clarifying 'laws of the land' include municipal ordinances.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX D — Comity principle: first-attaching jurisdiction should carry case; military retention discretion and prerequisites for attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: As a principle of comity, the jurisdiction which first attaches should carry the case to termination. For such jurisdiction to attach, the prisoner should be in custody and charges should have been served with view to trial by court-martial. Military authorities may decline to surrender until claims of the United States satisfied; retention of jurisdiction is discretionary and may be waived (especially for grave charges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: G.O.29; various C. and R. opinions (C.10048; 11589; 14042; 17767; numerous others) provide examples and factors for discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX E — Accused who desires to surrender should generally await formal application
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer or soldier accused, though willing to surrender himself to civil authorities, should not in general be permitted to do so but should be required to await the formal application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.31,622 (Sept., 1871) supports the practice to prevent self-surrender from circumventing procedural protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX F — 'Any of the United States' includes organized Territories
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'any of the United States' employed in this article properly includes any and all political members of the governmental system, and embraces an organized Territory equally with a State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.63,406 (Feb., 1894) cited as authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX G — Article is directory not jurisdictional; state or public authorities may apply in place of injured individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The article is directory not jurisdictional; it does not limit action to be taken by military authorities to cases where application is made by injured party. Where personal application impossible (e.g., murder), the State may take the place of the individual and make the demand; where indictment or warrant exists the State (in general sense) may make demand and commanding officer must surrender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.54,33 (June, 1892) and related cases illustrate state substitution for private victim applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX G1a — No US-funded transportation obligation for surrendered soldier to civil authorities' location
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no provision of law for transportation at the expense of the United States to the place where a surrendered soldier is wanted by civil authorities, even though surrendered on a legal warrant for a crime committed before enlistment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: C.1872; 7609; 13354; 13389; 17824; 18339; 18518; guidance explains practical logistics and financial responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX G1b — Reasonable condition that requesting State bear return costs after acquittal; no Army reimbursement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a State asks for the surrender of a soldier under the article, it is reasonable to condition surrender that the State bear the cost of returning the soldier in the event of acquittal or other non-conviction disposition. Held that no reimbursement can be made to the soldier for returning to his station out of Army appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.25219; P.57,277 (Jan., 1893) — recommendation and holdings on financial responsibility and recommended surrender conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX G1b (recommendation) — Attempt to impose condition that state return enlisted men if acquitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended that when enlisted men are surrendered and released at a distance from posts, the surrendering authority attempt to impose a condition that if the soldier is acquitted or the case disposed other than by conviction, the soldier be returned to his post at the cost of the authority to whom he was surrendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.25219 (June 30, 1909) — administrative recommendation to mitigate hardship on enlisted men.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX H — Article contemplates only officers/soldiers; does not apply to civilians on post; civil arrests on reservations a matter of comity
rubrics_metrics.description: The article contemplates only cases in which an 'officer or soldier is accused.' It does not apply to a civilian (e.g., Chinese laundryman) employed and residing at a military post; while desirable that civil arrests of civilians on reservations be made upon notice to proper commanding officer, such course is comity only and cannot be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P.112,134 (July, 1890) cited as example describing limits of article's scope vis-à-vis civilians.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX I1 — Article does not apply in time of war, but delivery of accused in capital cases may be allowed at discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: This article does not apply to a time of war; however, it does not forbid delivery of officers and soldiers accused of capital crime in time of war, but leaves the matter to discretion of proper authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.4916; 6613; 13499; 19855 — examples where discretionary surrender in wartime allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX I2 — Officers on leave and soldiers on furlough may be arrested as civilians
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer absent on leave or a soldier on furlough may be arrested in the same manner as any civilian, as they are not under immediate military control while so absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX I3 — Perjury not within 'person or property' offenses for surrender article
rubrics_metrics.description: Perjury is not an offense against the person or property of a citizen within the meaning of the fifty-ninth article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.26337 (Mar. 18, 1910) — excludes perjury from basis for surrender under article.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX K — Returned-on-bail soldiers must be made to appear for civil trial
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soldier surrendered under the article is released by civil authorities under bail and returned to duty, or escapes and returns to military custody, the department commander should instruct the commanding officer to cause him to appear for trial by the civil authorities at the proper time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.21,457 (June 16, 1866) — procedural obligation to ensure civil process continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX L1 — Retention of jurisdiction where federal criminal court or court-martial appropriate (ceded jurisdiction example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier on a military reservation ceded to the United States committed a killing, it was proper for the commanding officer to decline to surrender the soldier to state civil authorities, as jurisdiction vested in the Criminal Court of the United States for the district and in a legally constituted court-martial; if United States court takes jurisdiction by comity, military jurisdiction should be waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.17735 (Mar. 26, 1905) illustrates interplay of federal and military jurisdiction where territorial cession affects venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIX L2 — Department commander discretion to turn over scouts to civil authorities without court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where facts warranted belief that homicide amounted to murder and charges had been prepared as required by Army Regulations, it was within the discretion of the department commander to turn a Philippine scout over to civil authorities without bringing him to trial before a general court-martial; such action not contrary to regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C.21694 (July 9, 1908) — example showing discretionary transfer to civil authority even where military trial might be available.

rubrics_metrics.name: LX A1 — Duplicating pay accounts constitutes presenting false/fraudulent claim against United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The offense known as duplicating of pay accounts, which generally involves presenting or causing to be presented a false or fraudulent claim against the United States, is properly chargeable under this article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: B.37,356; 42,569; C.14619; 16131 — used to classify payroll fraud as an offense under the relevant article.

rubrics_metrics.name: LX A2 — Collusion with contractor and false vouchers constitute offense under article (misconduct in supply contracting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an officer colluded with a contractor who delivered less supplies than entitled while giving a voucher certifying delivery of the whole amount, such officer was chargeable with an offense defined in the article (8th paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.35,206 (Feb., 1876) — factual pattern for chargeable misconduct in procurement contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: LX A3 — Use of public property for private benefit constitutes misappropriation of United States property
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the Quartermaster Department using teams, tools, and other public property in his possession to erect buildings or otherwise for the benefit of a mainly civilian association of which he was a member was properly chargeable with misappropriation of property of the United States. Loaning public property to a contractor for purposes of filling a government contract likewise chargeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.10,664 (Dec., 1864); R.29,26 (June, 1869) — shows that customary local practice unauthorized by regulation is no defense though it may mitigate sentence if sanctioned by superior authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: LX A3a — Temporary private use of government animals: not embezzlement but applying property to own use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a quartermaster used temporarily, with his private carriage, a pair of Government horses in his charge, he was not properly chargeable with embezzlement but with the offense of knowingly applying to his own use and benefit property of the United States furnished for military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.4,421 (Dec., 1863) — distinguishes embezzlement from improper application of government property.

rubrics_metrics.name: LX A4 — Refusal to transfer public funds on lawful demand is prima facie evidence of embezzlement; burden shifts to disbursing officer
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5495 R.S. provides that refusal of any person charged with disbursement of public moneys promptly to transfer or disburse funds upon the legal requirement of an authorized officer is prima facie evidence of embezzlement. Applied to military cases, failure by a disbursing officer to turn over public moneys when required is prima facie evidence and the burden shifts to him to justify the proceedings; failure to account has resulted in conviction for embezzlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.22,548 (Jan., 1867) and the cited statute illustrate the evidentiary rule and its impact on military financial officers.
